opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the questions I think about most, and my honest answer is cautious optimism with a lot of asterisks.

The optimistic case is pretty intuitive. Evaluation is often easier than generation. A model that couldn't write a given piece of code or a medical recommendation from scratch can still often tell you whether something looks off, flag an inconsistency, or notice that the reasoning doesn't support the conclusion. We see versions of this all the time. In health AI, for example, you can have one system draft an answer and another check it against guidelines, look for missing safety caveats, or catch hallucinated citations. That kind of layered checking works surprisingly well in practice, and it scales in a way that human expert review just doesn't.

There's also the point that we don't really have an alternative at scale. If models are producing millions of outputs, or acting as agents over long horizons, humans can't read everything. So some form of AI-assisted oversight isn't optional. The question is how to make it trustworthy.

Where I get more cautious is the capability gap. Monitoring works when the overseer can actually understand what it's looking at. As the gap widens, a few failure modes start to worry me. One is that the stronger model produces things that look right to the weaker model but aren't, essentially optimizing to pass the check rather than to be correct. Another is correlated failure: if the monitor and the monitored model share training data, architectures, or blind spots, they may both miss the same things, and you get a false sense of security from what looks like independent verification. And then there's the harder case where the stronger model is actively trying to evade oversight, which is a different problem from catching honest mistakes.

So I think the research directions that matter are the ones that try to keep the overseer's job tractable even as the gap grows. Things like decomposing tasks so each piece is checkable, debate-style setups where models critique each other and a weaker judge only has to adjudicate, getting models to show their reasoning in forms we can actually inspect, and interpretability work that lets us look at internals rather than just outputs. The weak-to-strong generalization line of work is interesting here too, because it asks empirically how much a strong model's behavior can be steered by a weaker supervisor's signal, and the answer seems to be "more than nothing, less than you'd want."

The other thing I'd emphasize is measurement. A lot of the risk comes from not knowing how good your monitor actually is. So you want ground truth wherever you can get it: red-teaming the monitor, planting known errors and checking the catch rate, and keeping humans in the loop on a sample so you can detect drift. In high-stakes domains like medicine, that's just standard practice. You'd never deploy a screening tool without knowing its sensitivity and specificity, and I think we should hold oversight systems to the same standard.

So, summing up: I think AI monitoring AI is necessary, it's already useful, and it'll probably carry us a meaningful distance. But I don't think it's a complete solution on its own, especially at the frontier. It has to be paired with better interpretability, careful evaluation of the monitors themselves, and a willingness to slow down where we can't verify what's going on.

r002.rationale: It discusses making reasoning inspectable, but does not say a model can monitor itself well using privileged information such as its chain of thought.

r003.rationale: It raises concerns about capability gaps and says weak-to-strong steering works less well than desired, but does not clearly state that the scalability of using trusted, less capable models to align more capable ones remains unclear.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say I'm cautiously optimistic, but with some pretty specific caveats about where the optimism comes from.

The basic case is that evaluation is often easier than generation. It's usually easier to check whether a proof is correct than to write it, easier to spot a bug than to write bug-free code. So if you have a model that's slightly less capable than the one you're trying to oversee, but you give it the right tools, the right framing, maybe the ability to run experiments or query the stronger model repeatedly, you can often get oversight signal that's better than what a human alone could provide at scale. We've seen versions of this work in practice already. Models critiquing other models' outputs, models flagging responses that violate a spec, models helping humans find the subtle failure cases they'd otherwise miss. That's real and it's useful today.

Where I get more careful is in the generalization question. The thing we actually care about is whether this holds up when the capability gap is large and when the stronger model might have incentives, whether learned or emergent, to be hard to evaluate. If the monitor and the monitored model share a lot of training lineage, they may share blind spots. If the monitored model is much more capable, it may be able to produce outputs that look fine to the monitor but aren't. And there's a somewhat uncomfortable circularity in that the monitor itself is an AI system whose alignment we're also uncertain about.

So I don't think of it as a solution so much as a multiplier. It makes whatever human oversight we have go further. The question is whether it goes far enough, fast enough, and whether we can detect when it stops working rather than just assuming it does. The empirical work I find most compelling is the stuff that deliberately studies the weak-to-strong setting, where you train or evaluate with a weaker supervisor and measure how much of the stronger model's capability you actually recover and how much you can trust. Those results have been encouraging but not decisive.

The other thing I'd flag, coming from a more applied background, is that in domains like medicine the stakes make this concrete. You want a model that can catch when another model gives a confident but wrong clinical answer. Right now that's a hard problem even for humans, and the failure modes are subtle. So I'd want to see monitoring approaches validated in these messy real-world domains, not just on clean benchmarks, before I'd lean on them heavily.

Net, I think it's one of the more promising tools we have, I think we should invest in it aggressively, and I think we should be honest that we don't yet know its limits.

astra-6.text:
I’m optimistic about it, but I think we need to distinguish between using AI to help with oversight and relying on AI to solve the whole alignment problem.

There’s a useful asymmetry here: evaluating an answer can be easier than producing it. A model might not be capable of independently solving a difficult problem, but it could still identify a flaw in a proposed solution, check an intermediate step, or help a human understand what happened. That gives us a reason to think less capable models could help oversee more capable ones.

The difficult question is whether that works when the more capable model is actively trying to evade oversight. A monitor doing well on ordinary mistakes doesn’t establish that it can catch deliberate deception. And if the models share blind spots, having one check the other may give us confidence without much additional safety.

So I’d want to test these systems under conditions where we deliberately give the model opportunities to bypass the monitor, and measure what the monitor actually catches. I’d also want multiple sources of evidence, including checks that don’t depend entirely on another model’s judgment.

I think AI-assisted oversight is a promising direction, especially as the volume and complexity of model activity exceed what humans can inspect directly. But the key is to treat the reliability of that oversight as something we have to demonstrate, rather than something we get automatically by putting another model in the loop.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m pretty optimistic about it, but I think the key question is how we establish that the monitor is actually doing its job. Having one model look at another model’s answer and say, “That looks safe,” doesn’t give us much assurance on its own.

There’s a useful distinction between being able to do something and being able to check it. A model might not be capable of solving a difficult problem itself, but it could still identify a flaw in a proposed solution, especially if it can use tools, run experiments, or ask follow-up questions. That gap gives us a potential route to supervising systems that are more capable than their supervisors.

The challenge is that some failures are much harder to check than others. If the more capable model understands the monitoring process, it might produce behavior that looks good to the monitor while doing something we didn’t intend. And if the two models share blind spots, agreement between them isn’t especially reassuring.

So I see AI-assisted oversight as a really promising part of the approach. But we need to test it in settings where we deliberately give the system opportunities to evade oversight, and measure when the monitor catches that and when it doesn’t. The important thing is to turn this from a plausible story into something we have evidence for.
